Picks per station

Stations are triangles, positioned by longitude and latitude, sized and shaded by pick count. Coastline and state borders are drawn from Natural Earth for orientation. Hover a triangle for its code and count.

Station detail

Picks per month for one station, one line per campaign. The comparison is the point: western and global cover overlapping stations with different weights - original and jma_wc - so a station where one line moves and the other does not is the two models disagreeing, which no aggregate view shows. Both dropping together is an outage; both rising is a sequence.

The 500 stations with the most picks, monthly. Monthly because daily over 5,845 days does not fit in a page, and monthly is enough to see an outage or a disagreement.

Picks per day of data

Picks by the day the waveform covers — not by when the job ran.

Waveforms and picks

Picks drawn at random from the catalogue each hour, with the waveform they were made on. Only picks at confidence ≥ 0.5 are shown - the picking threshold is 0.2, so most of the catalogue is marginal and a uniform sample would mostly show that. Colour is the phase; the number is confidence. Traces are demeaned and high-passed at 1 Hz for display only - the picks were made upstream, on the data the model saw.

Campaign plan

What is still to run, costed from one measured rate: 0.0241 vCPU-hours per station-day (707 vCPU-hours over 10,440 station-days on the live SCEDC campaign, times 0.354 for the short-window amplitude rework), priced as vCPU-h x $0.031299/vCPU-h, derived from a real invoice. Time assumes the full 12,000-vCPU Fargate Spot quota with nothing else running. These are projections, not observations - the tiles above are what actually happened.

Two figures, and the difference is the hit rate. The rate above is per station-day processed; the plan counts station-days planned, and most planned days hold no data - measured hit rates run 21.7% to 67.6%. The upper bound column assumes every planned day has data; the expected column applies a 40% hit rate. The authoritative model, 24_cost_model.md, re-priced 2026-09-09 at the billed rate with western, obs and obs-early measured outright, put global at $9,450-$13,700 and the whole campaign at about $15,000 (a 2026-09-09 estimate, before the re-reads). Hit rates are measured for 61% of global's readable station-days, NP included at 0.5%; the rest sits on tier defaults.

As of 2026-09-09: the EarthScope restricted access point was never stalling: the credential request was unscoped, so it could LIST but not GET, and every read returned AccessDenied instantly. Scoping it to network=FDSN:<NET> fixed it, and restricted reads now run at 96-98 MB/s - the same rate as Open Data.

As of 2026-09-09, two things the plan still carries that will not produce picks: ~3.67M station-days on network-years EarthScope does not hold, which complete empty and are harmless; and 49 networks that answer 403, which were dropped from global on 2026-09-03 and can be restored if EarthScope grants access.

What it has cost estimated

Every figure in this section is an estimate, though a reconciled one. It is vCPU-hours, counted from Batch job start and stop times, multiplied by $0.031299/vCPU-h — a rate derived from a real invoice rather than a list price, by dividing a billed figure by the vCPU-hours measured over the same days. It bundles memory, logs, requests and addresses into the vCPU-hour, which holds only while the task shape does. The category split below is the estimate; the total is anchored to the bill.

This account cannot read its own cost data. Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost and Usage Reports and the Free Tier API are all denied by an explicit Deny in service control policy p-q1ngvul9 on organisation o-z3xgjt2s3d, whose management account is CloudBank via Strategic Blue. That is by design for a CloudBank-funded account: the authoritative cost lives in the CloudBank portal and its invoices, not in AWS. Recorded actual: $2,456.29 (2026-08-31/2026-09-06 $2,456.29), from costs_actual.json.

Where the catalogue lives

Public-read, no account needed. The picks are Parquet on S3, Hive-partitioned by network, year and month. Read them with anything that speaks Parquet; there is no database to connect to and no credentials to obtain. claims/ and progress/ are internal and stay private; picks, manifests and run provenance are open.

→ Open the tutorial notebook in Colab — installs, reads, plots, and re-queries the original waveforms from FDSN with ObsPy to draw the picks on the record.

buckets3://quakescope-picks-2026
regionus-east-2
pickss3://quakescope-picks-2026/<campaign>/picks/network=<NET>/year=<YYYY>/month=<MM>/<shard>.parquet
manifestss3://quakescope-picks-2026/<campaign>/manifests/<shard>.json
run metadatas3://quakescope-picks-2026/<campaign>/runs/<run_id>.json
pip install pandas pyarrow awscli

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Copy the partitions you want, then read locally. Measured on CI 2019-07
# (271 objects, 149 MB): sync 9 s + read 0.8 s, against 86 s for a
# filtered read straight from S3. Put network/year/month in the path;
# never glob picks/** (it lists every object in the catalogue first).
#
#   aws s3 sync --no-sign-request --region us-east-2 #     s3://quakescope-picks-2026/western/picks/network=CI/year=2019/month=07/ #     picks/network=CI/year=2019/month=07/

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_parquet("picks/")          # network/year/month become columns
ANON = {"anon": True}                  # for the small JSON reads below

# which model made them, and at what thresholds
import json, urllib.request
run = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(
    "https://quakescope-picks-2026.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/western/runs/"
    + df["rid"].iloc[0] + ".json"))

# or exactly the objects one shard wrote, from its manifest
m = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(
    "https://quakescope-picks-2026.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/western/manifests/<shard>.json"))
df = pd.concat(pd.read_parquet(f["path"], storage_options=ANON)
               for f in m["files"])

The three catalogues are global, obs (offshore stations only since 2026-10-03; the land stations' picks moved to _archive/obs-land/) and western. Earlier 2026 test and era prefixes (scedc, ncedc, earthscope, western-a, ...) are kept under _archive/, which is not public-read. The 2025 run is in a database, not in this bucket.

Columns. tid trace id NET.STA.LOC · cha band · pha P or S · peak the arrival time · conf model score, floored at 0.2 · amp Wood-Anderson displacement in metres · amp_vel peak ground velocity in m/s · start and end the pick window · rid run id, joins to runs/. conf is a detection score, not a probability of correctness; the 0.2 floor is permissive on purpose so you can pick your own threshold.

Manifests. records lists every station-day that reached the picker (tid, cha, yr, doy, npks). Shards run on image d0ccf9b or later also carry outcomes, one per planned station-day, with a status: loaded, no_data, no_channel, empty_read, not_found, denied, done (final), or refused, throttled, timeout, read_error, too_big (not read; queued for repair). That is how "no data" is told apart from "not read". Join the station table to picks on id = tid: until the 2026-10 fix the location_code column held floats such as 0.0 for 00.

Scoring picks against analyst arrivals

One script, two CSV files, no account and no AWS. score_picks.py imports nothing but numpy and pandas, takes the arrivals you trust and the picks a model emitted, and writes recall, precision, onset-time error, calibration and phase-swap rate. It is the same scorer that produced every number on the picker board, pinned by unit tests and byte-reproducible across runs.

→ scripts/score_picks.py — the command-line scorer · benchmark_metrics.py — the metric definitions, one function each · score_track_models.py — the batch version that scores many weight sets over many sequences

python scripts/score_picks.py --demo          # synthetic picks, nothing to download
python scripts/score_picks.py     --reference arrivals.csv \                 # station,phase,time
    --picks     mypicks.csv  \                 # station,phase,time,conf
    --out       scores/

Run your model once at a low confidence floor and keep every pick. Each threshold is then a filter over one file rather than another pass over the waveforms. The scorer refuses two mistakes rather than letting you publish them: station names that differ between the files, which would report a working picker as recall 0, and disjoint time windows, which is usually a time-zone error.

Against a bulletin, not every metric is available. Recall and the timing statistics are exact. Precision, F1 and calibration are lower bounds, because an unmatched pick may be a real arrival the analyst never marked; the scorer names those columns _lb. MCC needs true negatives, which a continuous record with an incomplete reference does not define, so it is not computed at all. → the picker board · downloadable benchmark data

Two pick counts, both true. The tile counts picks in shards that have finished, taken from their manifests. A running shard checkpoints its work to Parquet every 40 station-day-channels, so the objects on S3 already hold more than the tile shows; the manifest only appears when the shard closes. Query the Parquet for what is actually stored, the tile for what is durably accounted for. Every figure above except spend is counted from an S3 or Batch API response. Spend is derived: vCPU-hours from Batch job start and stop times, multiplied by $0.031299 per vCPU-hour. It is not a directly billed figure — Cost Explorer, Budgets and Cost and Usage Reports are all denied on this account by an explicit Deny in service control policy p-q1ngvul9, this being a CloudBank-funded account billed through Strategic Blue. The authoritative cost is CloudBank's, not AWS's, and it is recorded by hand in costs_actual.json when an invoice arrives. Data volume ingested from the archives is not shown because it is not measured anywhere; the catalogue size above is what was written, not what was read.
